---
title: "Critique of `01-qc.qmd` — what I would change and why"
format: html
---

This document reviews `01-qc.qmd`, the Study B quality-control report. It is
kept **separate** from that report on purpose: the QC report states what the
data are like; this one judges how the checking was done. Nothing here edits
`01-qc.qmd` — it is a list of findings, each with the evidence re-run from
scratch, and a final list of the changes I would make if I revised it.

Every claim below was re-computed against
`data/2-workshop2/group_b_contraception/` today, not copied from the report.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))

d    <- read_counts("group_b")
meta <- d$metadata
sp   <- d$species
gn   <- d$genes
```

## What the report gets right

These choices are correct and should not change:

- **Order checks with `identical()`, not `setequal()`.** Matching by exact
  position is the check that catches the failure mode that silently corrupts
  DESeq2 results. Re-verified: all three tables match the metadata order.
- **Flag, don't drop.** A QC report should report problems, not quietly
  reshape the dataset for every later document. Correct.
- **Checking `bv` against the Nugent ≥ 7 cut-off.** A label checked against
  the score it was derived from is a real QC catch, not busywork.
- **Every number I could verify is accurate.** B006 = 5,247 counts; 86 of 220
  species never observed; batch B2 RNA depth lower than B1 (median 12.0M vs
  13.7M). The report says what is true.

## Finding 1 — the metadata is never checked *against* the counts (the biggest gap)

The report checks that the six files **agree with each other** (sample IDs
match, in order) and that the metadata is **internally consistent** (`bv`
agrees with Nugent). Both are good checks, but neither answers the question a
mix-up would actually break: *do the sequences belong to the people the
metadata says they do?* Sample IDs can match perfectly across all six files
and still be attached to the wrong person's sequencing, because a swap at the
lab happens upstream of every file.

The cheapest guard is a biological sanity check: the counts should look like
what the labels say. For vaginal microbiome data, the obvious one is
Lactobacillus share against BV status — BV-positive samples are defined by
*losing* Lactobacillus, so a mismatch pattern here is a red flag.

```{r}
#| label: lacto-by-bv
# Lactobacillus share of each sample, split by the metadata's bv label.
rel  <- sweep(sp, 2, colSums(sp), "/")        # each column / its own total
lac  <- grepl("lactobacillus", rownames(rel), ignore.case = TRUE)
share <- colSums(rel[lac, ])

tapply(share, meta$bv, median) |> round(3)
cat("correlation of Lactobacillus share with Nugent score:",
    round(cor(share, meta$nugent), 2), "\n")
```

The result is exactly what vaginal-community biology predicts: BV-positive
samples have a median Lactobacillus share of **2%**, BV-negative samples
**97%**, and the share tracks the Nugent score with correlation **−0.84**.
So the metadata and the counts belong to each other — but the report only
learned this by accident, never having asked.

```{r}
#| label: lacto-plot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(data.frame(bv = meta$bv, share = share),
       aes(bv, share, colour = bv)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, size = 1.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "Metadata and counts agree: Lactobacillus collapses in BV-positive samples",
       subtitle = "One dot per sample; this pattern would break if samples or labels were swapped",
       x = "BV status (metadata)", y = "Lactobacillus share")
```

## Finding 2 — one median hides the bimodality

The report concludes: *"Lactobacillus (mostly L. iners and L. crispatus)
dominates the median sample."* The overall median share is `r round(median(share), 2)`
— technically true, but misleading. The distribution has **two humps**
(Lacto-dominated samples near 100%, BV-like samples near 0%), and a median of
0.57 sits in the empty valley between them, describing a sample that doesn't
exist. The report's own Finding 1 pattern is what makes the summary wrong.

The fix is one line: summarise **by group**, not overall — which is also
exactly the summary that doubles as the sanity check in Finding 1.

## Finding 3 — the two depth plots use different groupings, and the bar chart hides the tail

The report plots microbiome depth by **arm** and RNA depth by **batch**, with
no stated reason for the difference — and the metadata has only one batch
column (`rnaseq_batch`). A reader cannot compare the two tables, and neither
plot shows the interesting part of the data well: `geom_col()` draws 93 bars
per group on a **linear** axis, so B006 (5,247 counts, median 29,212) is a
nearly invisible sliver.

```{r}
#| label: depth-plot
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
depth <- rbind(
  data.frame(sample_id = colnames(sp), table = "Microbiome",
             reads = colSums(sp), arm = meta$arm, batch = meta$rnaseq_batch),
  data.frame(sample_id = colnames(gn), table = "RNAseq",
             reads = colSums(gn), arm = meta$arm, batch = meta$rnaseq_batch)
)

ggplot(depth, aes(batch, reads)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, size = 1.2) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.5, fatten = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ table, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Depth per sample, both tables, by sequencing batch",
       subtitle = "Log scale: each step up is 10x. Bars cross the group medians.",
       x = "Sequencing batch", y = "Total counts per sample (log)")
```

On the log scale the shallow tail is obvious at a glance, the two tables sit
side by side under the same grouping, and the batch difference in RNA depth is
still visible. The arm-vs-batch balance table the report already shows covers
the confounding question, so depth only needs to be shown once, one way.

## Finding 4 — a stated number with no code behind it

The report states *"88% of the cells are zero"* in its findings text, but no
chunk computes that number. It happens to be correct:

```{r}
#| label: zero-cells
round(mean(sp == 0), 2)
```

…but a document that reviews data quality should not contain a single
unsupported number. One line in the microbiome chunk fixes it.

## Minor notes

- **The all-zero-species check is framed as pass/fail** ("fewer than half the
  species rows are all-zero"), but 86/220 all-zero rows is not a failure — it
  is normal and only matters as a note to pre-filter before distance-based
  analyses. A check that cannot fail is not a check; state it as a note.
- **The cytokine section checks missingness only.** A one-line range summary
  per cytokine would guard against a units mix-up (pg/mL read as ng/mL, or a
  column in log units), which is the classic catch at this table.

## Changes I would make to `01-qc.qmd`

| # | Change | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add a Lactobacillus-share-by-BV-group check (and Nugent correlation) to section 2 | Only check that catches metadata↔counts swaps; IDs matching is not enough |
| 2 | Replace the overall "Lactobacillus dominates the median" sentence with the by-group summary | The overall median (0.57) describes a sample that doesn't exist |
| 3 | Replace both depth plots with one log-scale dot plot by batch, faceted by table | Same grouping for both tables; makes the shallow tail visible |
| 4 | Compute `mean(sp == 0)` in the microbiome chunk | No unsupported numbers in a QC report |
| 5 | Reword the all-zero-species item as a note, not a pass/fail check | A check that cannot fail is not a check |
| 6 | Add a per-cytokine range summary to section 5 | Catches units errors; costs one line |

## Choices made

- Kept this critique in a separate document (`01-qc-critique.qmd`) rather than editing `01-qc.qmd` in place — the alternative was patching the original, but a review should be readable alongside what it reviews.
- Re-ran every claimed number against the raw files before agreeing with it — the alternative was trusting the report's own output, which is exactly how an error in a QC report survives into every later document.
- Used Lactobacillus share as the metadata-vs-counts sanity check — the alternative was correlating microbiome vs RNA depth per sample, which catches file-level swaps but not label swaps, and is far less biologically interpretable.
- Showed Finding 2 as a jitter plot rather than a histogram — the alternative, a histogram of the share, shows the two humps but makes the per-sample comparison by BV group harder to read.
- Recommended a log-scale dot plot over the existing bar charts — the alternative was keeping bars with a log axis, but bars imply a summed quantity per category and 93 bars per group is visual noise.
- Kept the report's "flag, don't drop" philosophy and all of its existing *Choices made* section untouched — the alternative was rewriting for style, which is not the point of a critique.
